utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, the affirmation you made to tell the truth in your evidence still applies. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Berisha.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will continue with my cross-examination. After 1992 and 1993, do you know whether parallel authorities existed as set up by the Albanian population at that time?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my municipality there were no parallel authorities. The full authority there was exercised by the Serbian authorities. There were two segments of life that were organised by the Albanian citizens, and that was the health care and education. There was no other parallel government.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned health care and education. Were you personally involved in any of these activities and services?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't work in any of them. As I already said yesterday, I was involved in agriculture in order to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: After, as you put it, your expulsion from the municipality, did you have any problems with the Serbian authorities? And by that I mean political persecution or criminal prosecution or something of that nature.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only had a problem once when my late brother had a car accident, a POP, P-O-P, from Prizren clashed with him. And the police forces came and examined the situation, and I was taken together with him and my other cousin. The police took us and interviewed us. This was in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What do you do now, Mr. Berisha?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a pensioner. I work as a volunteer for finding out the truth about victims and missing persons. We have a coordinating council at the level of the whole country which deals with these issues, with the fate of the missing persons and victims. We still have 135 missing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You are doing this work together with Mr. Hysni Berisha, who testified here with you; am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He is the chairman of the organisation, and I am a member of the Presidency of the organisation. We help people who are looking for their loved ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you now to answer me this: While you were in Suva Reka and before you left Suva Reka before the war, were the Serbian forces and the army deployed in Suva Reka during the bombing if they were deployed there at all?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the bombing, starting from 1998, early June, the police forces were stationed in Suhareke, mostly in Hotel Balkan. The military forces were close to the dumper. We call it the dumper but it's a construction company close to that area. These forces would also move around but not very much. The police forces would move around a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: While you were in Suva Reka during the NATO bombing, did the NATO aircraft targeted the position of the police and the army? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The NATO forces only struck twice in Suhareke, once on a cafeteria owned by a Serb which was destroyed; the other one was on the bus company which was owned by the Nisavics. This was close to the forest. There were no other strikes in the town of Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, can you tell me roughly out of the 42 villages that existed in the area of Suva Reka municipality, how many villages were under the control of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not give you the number of villages; however, I can say that the villages on the right side of the road Prishtina-Prizren, Slapuzane, Peqan, Semetisht, Doberdelan were under KLA control. On the other part, only Budakove was under KLA control. The other villages were not under KLA control.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about the KLA giving orders to the local population to move based on the information available on the ground?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the KLA did not give any orders. The first order was given by the Serb police on the 28th of March around 1600 hours when the policeman Noi Gjura wearing a police uniform said we had to go to Albania because the other ones will come and we don't know who those other ones will be, and they will slit your throats. Those were his words, and at that time in town we could hear gun-fire, so the people started to leave. The KLA did not give any orders. The orders were given by the police. I mentioned only the example I know in my neighbourhood. The other people in other neighbourhoods received orders from other policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was this Djuro a local policeman?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was wearing police uniform, and he used to live in the neighbourhood, was a neighbour of ours before. I knew him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand from your evidence whether it was an order, whether it was a recommendation, or whether it was just a friendly neighbourly advice.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: His words were, Prepare to go to Albania because the others will come and they may slit your throats. These were his words, and I understand it as an order to leave the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Concerning my first question, I didn't get an answer from you. Do you know whether the KLA coordinated with the civilian population living in the villages around Suva Reka if they believed that the population was under a threat from the Serb forces and thereby instructing them to move out of that territory? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, the citizens of Suhareke, did not have any contact whatsoever with the KLA. We never received any order or recommendation from them to leave the town or the country. I don't know about the villagers because I did not have a chance to contact them, the villagers living elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Then I am not going to ask you any more questions about this topic. A minute ago you mentioned Mr. Misko Nisavic and his bus stop. Who was that man?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milorad Nisavic is his full name, but his pseudonym was Misko and people called him Misko of UDBA or of U-d-b-a. He worked in the same office since 1989. I knew him personally. I had contacts with him in 1989/1990 and also on the 16th of May, 1999, when he caught some relatives of mine, eight or nine of them and took them to the police station, and that was when I contacted with him, on the 16th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Nisavic was ever a commander or the chief of the police station in Suva Reka? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was chief of the secret service office, state security office, the Serbian service, not of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Zoran Lazic is?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know both of them, him and his brother. Their father was called Laza, their mother Vjera. Zoran was a driver. Later on he worked in the Territorial Defence Unit. I knew him well. He was born and bred in Suhareke and everybody knows what he did to Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When you know that everybody knew what he did to Albanians --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please repeat the question; the interpreters didn't hear the last part.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that he did all kinds of things to the Albanians and that everybody knew about that, what were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to his participation in the massacre of the 26th of March against the Berisha family, and now he's being tried in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have direct knowledge about this or is this a second-hand knowledge that you heard from witnesses or from judiciary in Belgrade concerning his activities?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say this because I have read the whole transcript of the trial in Belgrade, over 2.000 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, do you know who Dr. Boban Vuksanovic is?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His two name is Bobek Vuksanovic. People knew him as Boban. He's the son of Imer Shefrat, and his mother was called Nada. He was an illegitimate child. His father used to work at the Secretariat for Internal Affairs in Suhareke. I knew him from his childhood. When he became a doctor. And the last time I saw him, he was wearing a military uniform as a commander of the Crisis Staff for the Suhareke municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What position did he hold in civilian attire in March 1999 prior to the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: His last position was commander of the Crisis Staff for Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me what his civilian post was? Was he employed somewhere?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a doctor by profession. Whether he worked as a doctor or he dealt with other issues, I don't know that, because I was keeping my distance from the authorities. They know what they did. He worked in the municipality in the Executive Council then, later on he became mayor, and he also worked as the director of the health care centre in Suhareke. These are the positions he held that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Dr. Vuksanovic?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that he was killed on the 14th of April, 1999, on the road Suhareke-Mushtisht. He was killed on that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know under what circumstances he lost his life?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed in a car which people say had gone to -- on an inspection trip to Mushtisht. The four people who were in the car were in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was that a traffic accident or was he killed by gun-fire?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was killed by gun-fire. This was announced by his neighbours later on, after the 14th of April, the fact that he was killed by gun-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the people who were with him in the car, were they in police or in army uniforms?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was Dr. Bobek Vuksanovic one among the five people who entered the municipal building in 1991 and asked you to leave your office?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of the locals there was Boban Vuksanovic, Stanislav Andjelkovic, Tomislav Borisavljevic [as interpreted], and five other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was it Dr. Bobek Vuksanovic who succeeded you as the president of the municipality of Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision of the Assembly of Serbia did not decide who the mayor would become. The decision said that he would become chairman of the executive council of the municipality. He became mayor later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question for you today, Mr. Berisha, relates to your first statement in which you said - and you repeated the same answer to my learned colleague the Prosecutor - that at the border crossing, someone's ID cards were confiscated but some other people's cards were not. Will you tell me whether any criteria was applied and how this procedure was decided? Can you tell me some more about that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 21st of May, 1999, about 10.15 in the morning, in the house of my aunt where we were, a policeman came. At the moment I can't remember his name, Sinisa Andrejevic. He's a son of the Andrejevics who were teacher in the primary school. And he said, In 15 minutes you have to prepare and leave for Albania. He was with five other policemen. They were in uniform and carrying guns. And I asked him, Is this your decision or is it coming from higher up? He did not answer. He just said the same words, In 15 minutes you must leave for Albania. And from 11.00 to 2.00 when we reached the border crossing point, I was travelling with my brother and my cousin. There, a policeman and a soldier looked at the hands of all the people who were going through that crossing point, and that was how we crossed the border point and we went to Vrmice. In Vrmice there were policemen and soldiers who asked for our ID cards. I was taken -- my ID card was taken away, all the ID cards of my family as well. This was on the 21st of May, 2.00 in the afternoon, when we crossed the border to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement that you kept your ID card with you. Was that a mistake which you never actually corrected?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave them my ID card because the consequences could be dire if I didn't do so. Everybody else also had to hand over their ID cards. Some people also had to leave their cars behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will beg for another moment of your patience. Let me remind you, first of all, that the Prosecutor read out the summary, the 65 ter summary, and in the penultimate paragraph my colleague says the following: "Some of the people had their ID cards taken away from them, although the witness retained his ..." That's one thing. Then secondly - just a moment - your statement, Mr. Berisha, of the 17th of August, 2001 - again, it's the penultimate page in the statement in all languages, and in the second paragraph right at the end you say: "We headed towards Prizren and then towards Zulj. As we were leaving Prizren next to the drugs factory, a police officer and a soldier checked our IDs. They took IDs from some of the people, but they didn't take our IDs. So this soldier and this police officer took IDs from some of the people but they didn't take yours. And today you say something different. You signed this statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, if you read the next paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police took ID cards and driver's licences from all of us and removed licence plates from the vehicles. Yes, I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Here you say police yet you told us it was the military so which is correct? You've just told us that the military took your ID cards.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one policeman and one soldier there. At Farmakos area they took the IDs of some people; however, they took my ID and the IDs of the people who were on the same tractor with me at the border, whereas they took the ID cards of other people at Farmakos factory near Prizren. I was taken my ID card by them at the border crossing. They removed the registration plates, and they also confiscated the driver's licence from other people at the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just on this point but not referring to the witness's evidence specifically as he's testifying at the moment, I'd just like to refer to the summary that I read out in court which Defence counsel referred to. And I'd like to point out that the reference or the quote provided by Defence counsel does not reflect what I read out in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it is clear from the evidence that the witness spoke about two occasions when identification cards in particular were called for. On both occasions, according to my note, he spoke about a policeman and a soldier or police and soldiers; and he indicated that it was at the border that his identification card and all identification cards of those of his family were taken as well as vehicle registration. Is that a correct understanding of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is correct. About 5.000 people crossed into Albania on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This completes my cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. Ms. Gopalan, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Berisha.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I have some questions for you arising from Defence counsel's cross-examination. Yesterday you mentioned - this is at page 63 of the transcript - that the Albanian population was expelled from Mushtisht, Sopi, Vraniq, and Bukosh on the 2nd of April and ordered to go to Albania and that these villages were empty of Albanians. First I'd like you to clarify the names of these villages that you referred to. Which were the villages from which the Albanian population was expelled on the 2nd of April?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of April the following villages were emptied: Sopi, Mushtisht, Vraniq, Stavrove, and Bukosh, and Buzhalle.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: In which municipality were these villages located in?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them are in Suhareke municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisa, how did you find out that Albanians were expelled from these villages on this day?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Vraniq and Buzhalle that day and there I learned about this. Part of my family left from Buzhalle village on the 2nd of April. Two days and two nights later, they were returned; they were made to go back to Stavrove from Prizren area. Myself and my two sons, Luan and Shefqet, did not join the rest of the family but took shelter in the mountains in the area called Llanishte.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berisha. Just going back to your answer to my question on how you found out that Albanians were expelled from these villages, you say that you were in Vranic and Buzhalle on that day and that you learned about this. How did you learn about this when you were in those villages?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I escorted them up to Bukosh and Sopi, and I could see how they were leaving on tractors and other transportation means. And in Mushtisht, two or three days later, people had to move too. Some young men who did not join their families and who took shelter in the mountains told me that their families from Mushtisht had to leave because they were expelled by the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: How many people did you see being expelled in these areas approximately, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can freely tell you that there were more than 60.000 inhabitants in Suhareke municipality, with the exception of Gelance village, about 70 per cent of the villages were emptied. People were expelled and ordered to leave. I mentioned the 21st of May when I witnessed and was part of 5.000 people who crossed into Albania mainly from Suhareke municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And just taking you back to your answer about escorting the people from Bukosh and Sopi and that they were leaving on tractors and other transportation means. Did they tell you why they were leaving these villages?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't necessary for them to tell me. I could see that the offensive launched by the Serb forces was coming from Mushtisht in the direction of Popovan and Mushtisht; we were attacked with military equipment on the 2nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Do you recall what military equipment that you were attacked with?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was single- and double-barrel weapons that they used to fire and mortars too.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And when you say "they used to fire," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Serb police.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to move on to the 28th of March. You said yesterday at page 64 that after the 28th of March a large number of citizens were expelled from Suhareke, and you then went to Stavrove and Budakove. Now, in relation to these citizens who were expelled from Suhareke, how did you know that they were expelled on that day?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th of March, 1999, up until 7.00 p.m. I was in Suhareke and I could see the convoys leaving in the direction of Prizren. People were leaving in various transportation means. Myself and my wife, since we had no information about the fate of Jashar, we joined the rest of my family that left for Stavrove on the 25th. At 7.00 p.m., I met up with my family in Stavrove, whereas the rest of the relatives and cousins left in the direction of Prizren and later on to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berisha. Do you recall the number of people in the convoys that were leaving in the direction of Prizren?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which date do you have in mind, 28th or the 21st of May? On the 28th we did not count each and every citizen, but it was a large group, whereas for the 21st I was there myself, and I can tell you with full certainty that we were more than 5.000 people who crossed into Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha --

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who did not have transportation means were organised by Serb authorities to be taken by buses to Zhur.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. My question relates only to the 28th of March. Now, another incident that took place on the 28th of March you have also testified about. This was the destruction of the mosque in Suva Reka. Did the people leave Suva Reka before the mosque was destroyed or after, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After. The mosque was destroyed at 11.55 and the exodus started after 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could I call up Exhibit 614, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, you were asked yesterday about this mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could we go to the second page of this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: What is it you see in the second page?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the second page I can see the minaret that used to be there at the mosque and it's destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And this convoy that was leaving Suva Reka on that day, would they have passed by that destroyed minaret?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Close by the road because the mosque is near the main road that links Prishtina with Prizren. It's just a few metres above this road.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berisha. Just a few more questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you do, the -- only the first photograph was tendered earlier. You've now referred the witness to the second. I think we should have that in the same exhibit, which is I think Exhibit 614 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Moving on, Mr. Berisha. You also spoke yesterday about local Serbs being mobilised - this was at page 66 of your transcript. I have a few questions about these individuals who were mobilised. Now, what time-period are you referring to when you -- when you talk about the local Serbs who lived in your neighbourhood being mobilised?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After 1989, every now and then the local Serbs were armed and we knew this very well. They were mobilised into the ranks of the reserve forces. The mobilisation was carried out before June 1998. They were walking around in police and military attire because the main road that separated us -- we could see them very clearly reporting to the municipality building or the police station on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And who mobilised these local Serbs at that time?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The power was entirely in the hands of Serbia, the local authorities too. So it must be them who mobilised these locals. We had nothing to do with this mobilisation. We could only see them wearing uniforms and coming back from work or from the places where they were mobilised to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Berisha, you say that mobilisation was carried out before June 1998. How long did these local Serbs stay mobilised after the mobilisation was done in -- just before June 1998, as you say?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that date on until the war ended in June 1999, they were all dressed in police or military uniforms, especially the -- our neighbours, members of the Trajkovic and Krstic families.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berisha. And if you know, did such mobilisation only occur in your town in Suva Reka or did it occur elsewhere as well?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak about Suhareke proper because I didn't go to the towns nearby, Prizren or Prishtina, it was impossible for us to go there. So I can only speak about the town where I lived, Suhareke, where I could see this with my own eyes. My house is behind the municipality building, and they moved about in that area every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berisha. I understand. You were also asked some questions about uniforms when you were in Suva Reka - this is also at page 66 - and you referred to individuals wearing black clothes who had shaven heads. Could you clarify the time-frame when you saw these individuals?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw these individuals once I think before the coming, before the 24th of March. They came close to the petrol station in a Pinzgauer - this is how they called their vehicle - and they didn't behave in a normal manner, at least in my opinion. This is the only time I saw them. Later on it was impossible for me to go out on the main street and that's why I could no longer see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And after the 24th of March, who did you see in Suva Reka. You've just said that you no longer saw these individuals with the black clothes and shaven heads.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 24th to 28th of March, because on the 25th, as I said, there were killings in the centre of Suhareke. On the 27th, that is, on the 26th of March the massacre of the Berisha family was carried out. We were nearby. On the 27th of March, at around 4.00 p.m., the houses on the Rreshtan road, starting from the place where the massacre was committed were set alight. And I left for Stavrove on the 28th of March. I returned in Suhareke on the 29th of April, 1999 --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, if I could just stop you there and take you back to my question. You've described the events that happened between the 24th and the 28th of March. What I would like to know is who you saw participating in these events if at all you saw anyone.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was impossible for us to go near these sites where these events took place because we would have suffered. We would probably be in Batajnica or in morgues now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And by the events, you are referring to the killing of the Berisha family, am I correct, as you mentioned before?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Berisha, I have no further questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, you did mention during the questioning of Mr. Djordjevic that in the course of your voluntary work assisting to identify victims that there was still some 135 missing persons. Are they from the municipality of Suhareke or from the town or some other area? Could you help me?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 176 missing persons initially. Now we have 133 missing persons from the territory of Suhareke municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: You told us that a cousin of yours who lived close to the mosque told you that the minaret had been mined by the Serb forces. Do you recollect the name of that cousin at all?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Her name is Sala Elshani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, you'll be pleased to know that that concludes the questioning. The Chamber would like to thank you for coming again to The Hague and for the assistance that you have been able to give us, and you are now of course free to return to your normal activities. So thank you once again. The court officer will assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is the time when I think by the arrangement made yesterday we adjourn to resume at 11.15 to hear the next witness. So we now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please read aloud the affirmation that's shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Ms. Gopalan has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zogaj.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Please could you state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Shefqet Zogaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is your date of birth, Mr. Zogaj?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: On the 24th of May, 1972.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: In Bellanice.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And where do you live now, Mr. Zogaj?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: In Bellanice.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, did you provide two statements to the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY, the first one on the 26th of April, 1999, and the second on the 8th of June, 2001?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And have you recently had the opportunity to review these statements?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And having reviewed these statements recently, apart from a number of minor spelling errors, are you satisfied that these statements are true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zogaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender these two statements into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: They are respectively 65 ter 2322 and 2323.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 02322, Your Honours, will be assigned P00615; and 65 ter number 02323 will be assigned P00616, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, did you testify in the trial of Prosecutor versus Milutinovic et al. in this Tribunal in September and November 2006?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Have you recently had the opportunity to review your previous testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And having reviewed your testimony, if you were asked the same questions again would you provide substantially the same answers today?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender the witness's testimony in Milutinovic et al., that's 65 ter 5047.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00617, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in order to proceed efficiently with this witness, with your leave I would like to tender into evidence two associated exhibits that were referred to by the witness in his testimony in the Milutinovic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: These are 05048 and 05049.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 05048, Your Honours, would be P00618; and 65 ter number 05049 would be assigned P00619.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I would now like to read the witness's in-court summary. The witness is a Muslim male living in the village of Belanica in the municipality of Suva Reka. He describes the situation in Suva Reka from the 20th of March, 1999, when the OSCE-KVM mission pulled out from Kosovo. The streets were empty of Albanian civilians but there was a heavy presence of Serb and -- my apologies. There was a heavy presence of Serb police. On the same day, Serb forces attacked the villages in the area and people started to flee to safer places like Banja and his home village Belanica. As the inhabitants fled, they gathered in a big field in Belanica and by the 31st of March, 1999, there were a large number of civilians gathered in this village. On 1 April, 1999, Belanica was shelled and a large number of Serb forces entered the village. The Serb forces forced people from their houses and set the houses on fire. They were then -- the people were then forced by the Serb forces to leave Belanica in a convoy. The convoy was directed in two directions. During the trip, the convoy was stopped at a number of Serb check-points, where the civilians were beaten, robbed, and insulted. Members of the convoy arrived at the Albanian border, where their documents and vehicle plates were seized. That's the end of the witness's in-court summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, as you know, the Trial Chamber already has before it your previous testimony and statements, and therefore I'll just have a few clarificatory questions for you in relation to the events in Belanica on the 1st of April, 1999. In your statement you refer to the shelling of Belanica by Serb forces on the 1st of April, 1999. After the shelling, you say Serb forces entered Belanica. Could you tell us what these forces did when they entered Belanica, please?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: After the Serb forces entered Bellanice, in the beginning they started with the burning of the houses. At the entrance to the village about 60 men came out and they immediately started being beaten by the Serb police. Robbing of people took place, the expulsion of people, also people were being killed. At that time, about 80.000 people had gathered there from various villages from other municipalities such as Rahovec, Shtime, Lipjan, Suhareke, and Malisheve.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zogaj.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And these people who were gathered in Belanica, you say that they then formed a convoy and started to leave the village. You also say in your statement that the convoy was directed in two directions. Could you tell us in which direction this convoy was split into, in which two directions.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: The first direction was towards the village of Banja-Malisheve-Rahovec-Xerxe-Prizren-Morine. The second direction was Temeqin-Duhel-Suhareke-Prizren-Morine.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Which convoy did you follow, Mr. Zogaj?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: My family and I were in the Temeqin-Duhel-Suhareke-Prizren-Morine convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And these two convoys, where did they end up eventually?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: They ended up in Albania, in Morine, which is the border crossing point to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Zogaj, who was directing the convoys in these directions?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: The convoys were being directed by the police, the army, and Serb paramilitaries. They were armed up to their teeth.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Did they say anything to the members of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: There were constant insults, all kinds of swear words. They were swearing at NATO, Bill Clinton, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And did they do anything to the members of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes. People were beaten - I am one of them. They were people who were abducted. When we came back from Albania, we found them dead. Some of them were not found, they haven't been found to this day.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zogaj. I would now like to --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: You're welcome. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Let's move on to the events you experienced at the border crossing. Could you tell us which border crossing with you arrived at.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: We arrived at the Morina border crossing. After about 30 hours of travelling -- in normal conditions it only takes about one and a half hours. Our truck was stopped by a civilian who was wearing normal clothes. He had a side-arm, and he ill-treated us in various ways, and he took all our IDs and other documents. And he said, Don't even look at Kosova anymore. Kosova is Albania -- Kosova is Serbia. Go to Albania. Although we believed in our heart of hearts that we would be back in Kosova, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zogaj. Now, when was it that you arrived at the Morina -- at the border crossing in Albania?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: At the border crossing of Morina, we arrived the next day, on the 2nd of April, 1999, after 1500 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: When did you return to the village of Belanica, to your home village, after these incidents?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I returned to Bellanice on the 21st of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could I call up 65 ter 2345, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, there will be a photograph on your screen shortly, and I will ask you some questions about that photograph. Mr. Zogaj, do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: What does it show?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: This is my house burnt by the Serb barbarians.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: When was this photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: On the 21st of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And who took this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I personally took it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could we go to page 2 of this exhibit, please -- I'm sorry, page 3 in that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: What about this photograph, what does this show? Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: This photograph shows the basement of a house. This is where we had some -- our personal effects, and I also had hundreds of documents, my personal documents, school documents, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, where was this house located, in which village?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: In Bellanice, of course. It's my uncle's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now what about the rest of the village in -- of Belanica, what was the condition of the homes in that village?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: About 70 per cent of the village was burnt.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender the first two pages of this exhibit into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: First three pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- the second page appeared to be the reverse of the first.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I believe in that case I'd like to tender the first four pages of this exhibit because -- no, I stand corrected, the first three pages of this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00620, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, at this stage I do not have any further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gopalan. Now, Mr. Djordjevic, do you have cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Just give me a short time to prepare.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Zogaj. As Defence counsel, I will like to ask you a few questions, but I would like just to make some remark relating to the procedure. I don't know whether we were working under 92 bis. I would like to add that we have received from the Prosecution about 600 pages of documents in Albanian; however, these documents were not discussed today. Mr. Zogaj, can you please tell me before the NATO bombing began, were there any clashes between the KLA and the Serbian forces in and around Belanica, your home village?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: There were none in Bellanice. Before the clashes started, the Serb police and army and paramilitaries killed and massacred the civilian population, the Albanians, innocent people. Those who could leave came to our village; the others took to the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me stop you, please. What you are talking about now is something that you already gave evidence -- or actually, this is contained in your statement. For the sake of time at our disposal, I would kindly ask you to give me as brief answers as possible to my questions. I asked you whether you know if there were any clashes between the Serbian forces and the KLA, yes or no; or if you don't know ...

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: There were no clashes in Bellanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Prior to the beginning of NATO bombing, you personally, as a journalist, were you aware of the incidents in which members of the Serbian families were abducted by the KLA and the Albanian separatists?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Could you ask the question again, please. I'm not clear what you're asking. I didn't understand it. And then I will give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Given that you are a journalist and you said that you worked for Bujku magazine and Rilindja publishing house, do you know that before the bombing started if there were any abductions of Serbs in Kosovo committed by members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: In the territory where I operated, there were none.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any knowledge of the killings of members of the police prior to the NATO bombing, regardless of their ethnicity? So I'm referring to police officers in Kosovo and Metohija, and I'm also asking about whether they -- you know that they had been killed by members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge of these cases, and you never admitted or accepted -- even when there were any such killings, you never accepted that there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what you wanted to say, Mr. Zogaj. When you say "we never," can you please specify who is "we." I really didn't get your point.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: We Albanians, during the time of the Serb occupation from 1989 to 1999, I don't know of any other killings except for the killings of Albanians. Even if there were any other cases, you never admitted to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, if I could interrupt. You will understand that in this Court counsel has a role to perform to represent an accused on the one hand and to represent the Prosecution on the other. That does not mean that they are the accused or the Prosecutor. They have a role to fulfil to assist us. If you want to speak about actions by Serb forces, if you could refer to them. Don't address counsel as though he was a member of those Serb forces or police. He was -- he is not here in that capacity. He's here to assist us. So if you could observe that distinction and show that respect for the Court and the counsel. You grasp what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll proceed with my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, my next question is: Do you have any information about the killings of respectable and prominent Serbs in the area where you lived? I'm talking as of the beginning of NATO bombing period.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Honestly, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me, do you know or are you able to describe -- first of all, tell me, Belanica, the village where you were born and where you lived, was it controlled by the KLA or by the Serb forces during the NATO air-strikes, so from the 24th of March, 1999, onwards?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: From the 24th of March until 1st of April, 1999, Bellanice was a village between two fires. The war had not started there yet. Until the 28th of March KLA members were there, whereas the fighting was going on somewhere else, in Dulje, Bllace, Peqan, Suhareke, Dragobil, and Banja. Bellanice was a calm place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to tell me what villages around Belanica were also controlled by the KLA, and what villages near Belanica were controlled by the Serb forces, if that was the case at all.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Under KLA control were the following villages: Banja, Kravoseri [phoen], Pagarushe, Semetisht, Bllace, Temeqin, Lladroviq, Guncat, and Senik, whereas under Serb control were the following: Malisheve, Dragobil, Duhel, Suhareke, and other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zogaj. And could you now tell me this: What uniforms, if any, were worn by the KLA members in the area where you lived, if you can describe them?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: They had military uniforms. I don't know where they got them from; however, they also had civilian clothes like I'm wearing now, because it was very difficult for them to provide each and every member of the KLA with a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell me what kind of weapons did the KLA members have in the territory where you were?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Basic and simple weapons - I don't know if any other army in the world has such weapons - basic weapons, Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any movements of people - I'm asking about the Albanian population - that had been pre-arranged by -- with the KLA based on the situation in the field or on the ground? I'm asking you about March 1999 until the end of the conflict; in other words, until June 1999. Were there any movements of Albanian civilians that had been pre-arranged with the KLA because of the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The KLA never did such a thing. It was impossible for the KLA even to protect the population because they didn't have the means necessary for protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: If there was an imminent threat by the Serb forces, did the KLA withdraw from the territory it held until that time together with the civilians?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: The KLA had its own fighting positions. It was impossible for them to defend these positions because the Serb forces, military police, and paramilitary had sophisticated weaponry including aircraft. Therefore, the KLA had to move from one location to another location to quieter and more peaceful areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you just answer my question. Did the KLA do that together with the people; in other words, when the people moved?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: The people were withdrawing because bombs were falling amidst -- in their midst, bombs from far, and they had to take shelter somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you've already explained that. It's already on the record, from your testimony in the Milutinovic and Milosevic trials and from your statement. My question is: When the KLA had to withdraw, did it withdraw together with the columns of the people?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: The Kosova Liberation Army withdrew on their own, because had the population withdrew -- withdrawn with them, 80.000 people wouldn't have been caught in Bellanice and sent to Albania. There was not a single member of the KLA in Bellanice on 1st of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You mean to say that among the 80.000 people there was no -- there was not a single KLA member? Is that what you're saying? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: On the 1st of April, 1999, there was not a single member of the KLA amongst the population. They were in the mountains. They had abandoned their fighting positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zogaj. We heard you say that you were a journalist, that you worked for Rilindja and for another magazine. Can you please tell us, when did you become a journalist in Rilindja?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I started writing articles in 1996. At that time only Bujku was operational. Rilindja had been closed down in 1990, but we found our way of operating and writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, at the time when you worked as a journalist in 1999, did Rilindja still exist as a publishing house and the Bujku newspaper or not?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: That was the same thing, Bujku and Rilindja were the same thing. Bujku was created as in 1990 Rilindja was closed down. So we found a way to assist the population and inform the population, and we converted Rilindja into Bujku. It was a well-known newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In 1999 did Bujku exist?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: At that time it had started to convert again from Bujku into Rilindja. After the beginning of the NATO bombing, it was not published at all. It began being published again after we returned from Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to get from you an answer. This newspaper, be it Bujku or Rilindja, was it registered as a public medium officially in 1999 in accordance with the valid legislation of the Republic of Serbia and the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: The editor-in-chief is the competent person for these issues. I was a simple journalist. I would bring information to the office, the information was published. If something had remained unclear, they would consult their people on the ground. This is how it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well I understand that you have no knowledge of that. My next question is: Did you receive any salary for the work that you put in?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zogaj, do you know anything about any parallel institutions and authorities of the Albanian citizens in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: From 1989 we, the Albanians in Kosova, were active in different ways to the extent we could because we were stripped of all our rights. The constitution of 1974 was forcefully revoked by the Serb authorities; however, we had to work and inform the international public opinion about what was going on in Kosova. This was the only way to get where we are today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So there were parallel authorities and institutions. What do you know about that specifically?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: We were expelled from our schools, from our work, from every institution that existed there before 1989, that is, that existed in Kosova. All our rights had been taken away and given to Serbs. They enjoyed all the rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, you spoke about that, but what I'm interested in is what parallel institutions existed in Kosovo and any authorities, if they existed, to tell me what you know about that, or is it the case that you don't know anything?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: The Democratic League of Kosova was created by the now-late President of Kosova Ibrahim Rugova. The institutions were established in Kosova and in the diaspora, lead by prominent people of Kosova, Bujar Bukoshi; Fehmi Agani, now passed away. Then the new education system was set up, new schools were opened, those that were taken away by the Milosevic regime. This is how the education system worked. We were mainly organised in private houses, not in proper school buildings. Fortunately now they have been given back to the Albanians in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And light of the fact that you're a journalist, do you have any knowledge about the St. Edigio agreement about the return of the Albanian students to the Pristina university and the return of some elementary and secondary schools into the Serbian school system, that's the year 1998/1999, on the eve of the air-strikes against Serbia and the whole of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I do have knowledge about this. This was an effort of the international community, a pressure on the Serb government. They had to release and put at our disposal, according to this agreement, all school institutions and buildings. However, the agreement was never implemented. Milosevic insisted on signing the agreement, but he never implemented it in real terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Partially, partly implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question for you, Mr. Zogaj, is this: Did you personally participate in any parallel system of government at that time?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I want to point out the fact that in 1990 Albanian students were poisoned by certain Serbs, and this is how it all started, the separation of Albanian and Serb students in terms of education. I was amongst the students who were poisoned, and I was part of those who were expelled from proper school buildings and had to continue my education in private houses. Then I joined the LDK in the village and was active in different ways, initially by collecting funds to pay the teachers because the teachers were not getting any salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any problems with the Serb authorities for that reason or for any other reason? I am referring to any criminal prosecution or perhaps some misdemeanour proceedings against you or anything of the sort, against you personally.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: In 1990 I was poisoned. I was in secondary school, third year, in Malisheve. In 1994 I was robbed by the regular police, Serb police, I was beaten too. Again, in 1994 in Prishtina I was beaten by the Serb police just for having on me a writing that was being prepared for publishing in the monthly Bota e Re magazine, which was a student magazine. I was beaten by the Serb police solely for this reason. I was again beaten on the 5th of May, 1998, in Duhel. They beat me for about 37 minutes. It's Duhel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were any proceedings instituted against you at all?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me, what do you do today, now? How do you make your living?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: At the moment, I have a small business.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you still in journalism?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Not at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard you say that you were poisoned in Malisevo while you were in secondary school, but was it not the Pristina university that was targeted by poisoning and not the Malisevo secondary school? Could you please elaborate this a little bit.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I will elaborate it a bit more. Not only in Malisheve secondary but also in Suhareke, Prishtina, and Podujeve, almost in every secondary and primary school a kind of poison was thrown by the Serbs. I fell ill together with 7.000 pupil and students of different ages as a result of this poison that was thrown in different schools, primary and secondary schools. At the time, the regular police did not allow us to go to the nearest health clinics for treatment. This is a reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell me that only ethnic Albanians got sick in schools while Egyptians, Turks, Romas, and Serbs remained healthy - am I right? - throughout Kosovo, not only in Malisevo and in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I don't know what happened to other students, but there was a policy of segregation between Albanian and Serbian pupils. They were working in shifts. Let's say Albanians will attend school in the morning, the Serbs in the afternoon, and vice versa. I will give you the example of an 11 year old, a Serb. In Prishtina, in the clinic there where I was also admitted, I was told about [as interpreted] his mother about what had happened to her child. This was an attempt by the Serb authorities to extinguish a whole generation of students and pupils.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether any such events - because I personally was not aware of any such incidents - resulted in criminal prosecution of persons responsible? Is there any evidence obtained, either by the international community or by some Serb organs that the Serbs authorities or Serbs were responsible for that? How do you know that it was the Serbs who did it?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: It's a known fact. The international community carried out the analysis and they designated the type of poison. The Serbs were preventing the examinations in the institutions in Prishtina and Prizren. Only samples that could be taken abroad were examined and analysed. If you want to find out more about this, you can search the archives in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will not dwell on this anymore. You mentioned the Serb forces that came into your village. Could you tell me what kind of uniforms did you see at that time while you were in Belanica? How did the uniforms worn by the Serb forces look like?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Police had the police uniform; the army had the military uniform; the paramilitaries had different types of clothes, shaven heads, head-scarfs, different types of weapons, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the people with shaven heads, what kind of uniforms did they have? Was there anything peculiar, something that struck you?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: They resembled paramilitaries, i.e., the people with the shaven heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, was there anything peculiar about the weapons that those people, people with shaven heads that you can -- that you thought were paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: They had the same type of weapons as the police and the army. They also had pliers and other instruments that are used to fix machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, among the members of the Serb forces who wore uniforms, were there any such members that you or your fellow villagers or generally people in Belanica managed to recognise?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, there was a policeman who was known to the whole village, Zika. He was known in Bellanice, Bllace, Temeqin, and so on because he used to patrol there at the time when the war had not yet come to Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any men, any Serbs, from the local area who had not been members of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: There was one from the village of Banja who had joined the Serb forces. He was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So he was a policeman too. Generally speaking, in and around your village were there any Serbian households, any Serbian families living there?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: In my village there were no Serbs. In Banja there was one Serb household, but they moved to the Serb side. In the other villages around Bellanice there were no Serbs - I'm not speaking about Suhareke here, I'm speaking about Bellanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are there any Serbian families living still there, for example, in Suva Reka where they used to live? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I don't know of any Serbs in Suhareke now who used to live there before because they know what they did to the Albanian population, and that's why they don't come back. Our government structures today are working with the whole people, with the entire population, but they have not come back. We are equally working with Serb minority, the Roma minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the man called Milorad, a.k.a., Misko Nisavic is? In your first statement given in Tirana, Albania, he mentioned him not by the name of Nisavic but Milorad Miskovic, which you later corrected and confirmed that his last name was actually Nisavic. What do you know about this man?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Miskovic used to have a driving school. The civilian population knew him very well. Later on, Misko Miskovic, Nisavic, these were his nicknames. His real name is Milorad Nisavic; the others are nicknames.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what did you mean when you said that he was the chief of the police station in Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, he was the chief of the police station. He was known by all as a policeman; but instead of exercising his duties as a policeman, he killed Albanians in the end, mercilessly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Who is Zoran Lazic?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: He was also a killer in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you, in your statement given in March you said that he was the chief in the municipality; then you in February 2003 changed that and said that he was the greatest and the worst criminal in Suva Reka; then on the 22nd of September, 2002, and I think it is given in the supplemental information said that he was a member of the army and the command and that you heard about him from the KLA. So you first described him as the chief of the municipality, the worst criminal, and then the member of the army. Can you tell me which of all these qualifications are -- is correct.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: The fact that the Serbs overnight made him chief of the municipality, director, and everything else cannot be forgotten. And that does not exclude the fact and the possibility that he committed crimes. The Albanian people were in a miserable situation. Children and old people, the elderly, were not spared by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: He was never president of the municipality. This Zoran Lazic, whom you qualified as the worst criminal in Suva Reka, did you know him personally or did you acquire this information, as you said, in September 2002 from the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I did not know him personally; but in my cooperation with the KLA, they told me what crimes he had committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally know Misko Nisavic or had you only heard of him from other people?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I did not know him personally. However, I'd like to mention Seidi Bytyqi, the history teacher who was abducted by Misko Nisavic, and Misko had ordered for this group of people he was with to be killed. Seidi fled the site of the tragedy and hid himself in a sewer, where he had stayed for five or six hours. I took this information from Seidi Bytyqi, who later on left Suhareke. I know Seidi very well, and he can give a statement or testify here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that as well in your previous statements and testimonies. Do you know anything about a person known as Boban Vuksanovic or Dr. Bobek Vuksanovic from Suva Reka? Do you know who I'm referring to or you don't?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I don't know this person. I don't know anything about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you cooperated with the KLA in response to my question about Zoran Lazic. How did this cooperation with the KLA look like? What did it imply and include? And how long did it last?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: We were not able to receive information from the Serb police, army, and authorities. They wouldn't give us any kind of information on anything that was happening in Suhareke or anywhere else. The only cooperation that we had was by personally observing the territories where the KLA operated, and from there I could see the shelling and the fighting conducted by the Serb police and army forces against the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you consider yourself to have been a member of the KLA at the time?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I never was a member of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zogaj.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I feel honoured to have been able to cooperate with them, but not as a journalist of the KLA. I was an independent journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question is: Do you have any information about the KLA's organising Territorial Defence or civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Of course that there was defence. It had to be organised because we were oppressed all the time by the Serb police. We didn't have the right to move from the 1990s until the liberation of Kosova. Every time we moved, we were scared; and torture and killings ensued only because we were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that you didn't understand me correctly, but I will conclude that you have no information to offer in response to my question. Next question: What armed formations, whatever they were called, were present in the area where you lived?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: That's your opinion. In my area, I mentioned the villages earlier where the KLA operated, but on the 28th of March there were no members of the KLA in Bellanice --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't understand me. I'm asking you if you know what -- which KLA units were in that area. If you know, tell us their names, the number of the brigade and what the names they had if you know; if you don't know, then ...

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: In our area, the 121st Brigade, the Kumanova Brigade, was operating; the other part in Semetisht, the 123rd Brigade was operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, do you know who the commanders of the 121st and 123rd Brigades were? Do you know their names?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: Fatmir Limaj was a commander of the 121st Brigade, if I'm not mistaken; commander of the 123rd, I can't give you the exact name now, Commander Drini I think, but I'm not sure. I know, however, that the 123rd Brigade was operating there. This because their names were not given to us at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Bislim Zyrapi was and what position he held?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: I did not have any contact with Bislim Zyrapi before. I only met him here in the Tribunal. I know him by name, but I don't know what his position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: If that is the case, sir, I'm not going to ask any questions of this nature. My last question today: In your first 1999 statement you said that you filmed a lot of footage with your camera but that unfortunately all of this material was burned in your cousin's house -- actually, that was your statement given in 2000. But in your first statement given, I think, in Tirana you mentioned that a Sanyo camera, tapes, and a Dictaphone that you were given as a present were confiscated from you by the police. So in order to avoid any confusion, can you tell us which version is correct and accurate. Did your camera and all the material burn in the house, as you said in 2000; or was the camera, the tapes, and everything else confiscated from you back in 1999 while you were leaving the area of Kosovo and Metohija and that it was done by the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET ZOGAJ
utterances.text: The fact is that the documents I had - and there were tapes there, photographs as well which I had put in my uncle's basement for protection - and they were burned. But the other ones, when I was caught by the Serbian police, the camera and every other thing that you mentioned were confiscated by them. Unfortunately, money can open doors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... cross-examination with this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. Is there re-examination, Ms. Gopalan?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: No re-examination, Your Honours. But I do have a message to convey to Your Honours from the witness that's unrelated to his testimony directly, but just an apology in relation to the attire that he is wearing at -- in court today. With your leave, he requested me to convey his apologies. He said that he would have preferred to have worn more formal clothing, but due to a shortage of time he wasn't able to change, and he would like to convey his deepest apologies to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gopalan. That was not necessary, but thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Zogaj, the Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance yet again here in The Hague and for the assistance you've been able to give. You will, I gather from what has been said, you have been told that we are following today a shortened procedure, and we also have received the statements that you have made and the transcript of your evidence when you came here last time so that between that material and what you have said today we will have a very complete account of the events about which you were able to speak. So we would thank you for all of that and for your continuing assistance and cooperation. You are now, of course, free to go back to your ordinary activities and the court officer will show you out, but you go with our thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Gopalan, are there some procedural matters?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This is in relation to the four witnesses that the Chamber ruled were not required to appear for cross-examination. This is your decision of the 16th of March, 2009, and in paragraph 41(D), the Chamber orders that the four witnesses are not required to appear for cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Right. Do you now propose to tender their statements?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The statements of Fazliu Fondaj, that is Hamide Fondaj, Ali Hoti, and Florim Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: That's right. I propose to tender their statements and associated exhibits as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I will begin with Fazliu, Hadije, 05033.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00621, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00622.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00623.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00624.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00625.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Before I proceed to the next witness, would the Chamber like me to read out an in-court summary of this witness's evidence?
